title: India's KochVac TB Vaccine Candidate Targets Human Trials by Mid-2027
excerpt: The protein subunit candidate from IIT Bhubaneswar and the Institute of Life Sciences, patented on November 16 and licensed to TechInvention Lifecare, is being studied as a possible BCG booster — with no human efficacy data yet.
body:
• An Indian tuberculosis vaccine candidate developed by IIT Bhubaneswar and the Institute of Life Sciences, known as KochVac (Hsp16.3ΔC4), is targeting the start of human clinical trials by mid-2027.
  • It is a protein subunit vaccine built from an altered form of Hsp16.3, a protein of the TB bacterium, and is being studied as a possible booster to BCG, which protects adolescents and adults poorly against pulmonary TB.
  • The candidate was granted an Indian patent on November 16, 2026, and has been licensed to Mumbai-based TechInvention Lifecare, which is preparing further preclinical studies and compliant manufacturing.
  • Nothing is yet known about whether it works in people: there are no human trial results, and the mid-2027 date depends on completing the additional studies, manufacturing work and regulatory approvals.

A tuberculosis vaccine candidate developed in Bhubaneswar is being prepared for its first tests in people. Scientists at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Bhubaneswar and the Institute of Life Sciences (ILS) have developed a protein-based candidate, known as KochVac, that could move into human clinical trials by mid-2027 following results in laboratory mice, according to Medindia's report on the programme.

The candidate, designated Hsp16.3ΔC4, is built from an altered form of heat shock protein 16.3 (Hsp16.3), an antigen associated with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the bacterium that causes TB. Unlike BCG, which is a live attenuated vaccine, it is a protein subunit vaccine — it contains a selected protein component rather than a whole live organism — designed to stimulate both cellular and antibody-mediated immune responses.

The gap it is meant to fill

BCG, the century-old vaccine given to infants, offers limited protection against pulmonary TB in adolescents and adults — the form of the disease that drives transmission. KochVac is being evaluated as a potential booster for exactly that age group. That advantage is still a research hypothesis: whether the candidate protects better than BCG, or works effectively as a booster, can only be established through human clinical studies, and no human efficacy data exists yet.

"We recently consulted a group of experts and based on those interactions, we are generating more and more data. We will go for human trials by mid-2027."

— Syed S Ahmed, Director and CEO, TechInvention Lifecare, to Business Standard

Who is doing what

The engineered protein was developed by a team led by Professor Ashis Biswas at IIT Bhubaneswar, and its preclinical evaluation in mouse models was carried out at ILS. Biswas has described it as India's first indigenously engineered TB vaccine candidate. The researchers received an Indian patent for the vaccine composition on November 16, 2026.

Mumbai-based TechInvention Lifecare Limited has licensed the technology — the transfer was facilitated by the National Research Development Corporation (NRDC) — and is generating the additional preclinical data needed for clinical development while preparing production processes that meet Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) and Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) requirements, according to reporting of the Business Standard account. The company is also working on novel adjuvants intended to improve efficacy.

An independent check abroad

The candidate has also been selected for further evaluation under the European Union-funded TBVAC-HORIZON programme. According to an IIT Bhubaneswar institutional update, that evaluation is intended to use a mouse aerosol-infection model at the UK's Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) — an independent animal-model check of the candidate before human testing.

What to watch

The mid-2027 target is a plan, not a result. The start of human trials depends on completing the additional preclinical studies, finishing the manufacturing preparations and securing regulatory approvals. Readers should treat any claim about how well KochVac works as unproven until human trial data is published: the honest summary today is a patented, licensed candidate with encouraging mouse results and a dated plan to reach the clinic.
nri_angle: TB remains a major health burden in India; an indigenous booster candidate matters to diaspora families with relatives in high-burden regions.
